blurb: One model, thousands of chips: the ways to split the work, and how to keep a giant training run going when hardware keeps breaking.

steps.h: One GPU is far too slow
steps.p: Training a frontier model on a single GPU would take centuries. The work has to be shared across thousands.
The simplest split: give every GPU a full copy of the model, and a different slice of each batch of training text.

items: Batch of text split into slices
Each GPU: same model, its own slice

steps.p: Each GPU works out how the model should change from its slice. They average their answers, and every copy makes the same update — staying identical.
steps.analogy: Ten students each mark a tenth of the exam papers, then pool their notes on common mistakes.

steps.p: Training needs far more memory than just the parameters: gradients and the optimizer's notes too — about 16 bytes per parameter. A 7-billion-parameter model needs about 112 GB.

visual.caption: Memory for a 7B model in training.

steps.p: Sharding (ZeRO / FSDP) splits all that memory across GPUs instead of copying it, fetching pieces only when needed.

cards.q: What's the main limitation of plain data parallelism?
options: The whole model and its training memory must fit on every GPU
It gives a different answer than one GPU
cards.hint: Every GPU holds a full copy.
cards.why: Everything must fit on each GPU. Fine for small models; impossible for a model needing hundreds of gigabytes.

cards.q: Training needs about 16 bytes per parameter. Roughly how much memory does a 7-billion-parameter model need?
cards.why: About 112 GB. 7 × 16 = 112. That's more than one 80 GB GPU holds — before even counting working memory.

cards.statement: Data parallelism gives the same result as training on one giant GPU with the whole batch.
cards.why: True. Averaging the slices' gradients is mathematically the same as computing them all together. It just runs faster.

cards.title: Microsoft's ZeRO technique removed the wasteful copies that data parallelism keeps.
cards.detail: Introduced in 2019 in DeepSpeed, it splits optimizer notes, gradients and even parameters across GPUs, fetching pieces only when needed.

cards.q: Fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP) saves memory by…
options: Splitting the parameters, gradients and optimizer notes across GPUs instead of copying them
cards.why: Sharing, not copying. Each GPU stores only its share and borrows the rest briefly when it's needed.

cards.title: Cutting the model itself into pieces

steps.p: Each big matrix multiplication is divided across several GPUs, which each do part and combine results — many times per layer.
steps.analogy: Four people each adding up one column of a giant spreadsheet, then combining totals.

steps.p: Because GPUs swap results constantly, this is usually kept inside one server, where GPUs are joined by very fast links like NVLink.
Different GPUs hold different layers. Data flows from one group to the next, like an assembly line.
At the start of a batch, later stages wait with nothing to do; at the end, early stages do. That idle time is the pipeline bubble.
Splitting each batch into many small micro-batches keeps every stage busy most of the time.
steps.analogy: A car factory sends cars through one after another, not one car all the way before starting the next.

cards.q: Why is tensor parallelism usually kept within a single server?
options: It needs extremely frequent, fast communication that only links inside a server provide
cards.why: Constant chatter. GPUs exchange results many times per layer. Slower links between servers would leave them waiting.

options: Idle time when stages wait for work at the start and end of a batch
cards.why: Waiting time. Like an assembly line warming up and winding down. Micro-batches shrink it.

cards.statement: Pipeline parallelism needs less communication bandwidth than tensor parallelism.
cards.why: True. Stages only pass results along at layer boundaries, so it can stretch across servers.

cards.title: Meta trained its 405-billion-parameter Llama 3 using four kinds of parallelism at once.
cards.detail: On about 16,000 H100 GPUs it combined tensor, pipeline, context and data parallelism — splitting matrices, layers, long sequences and batches all at once.

cards.statement: NVIDIA's Megatron-LM work helped popularise tensor parallelism for transformers.
cards.why: True. Its 2019 paper showed how to split transformer layers neatly across GPUs, and the approach became standard.

steps.p: Mixture-of-experts models have many "expert" sub-networks. Expert parallelism puts different experts on different GPUs.
Each token must travel to whichever GPU holds its chosen expert and back — an "all-to-all" shuffle of data across the cluster.
steps.analogy: A sorting office where every letter may need to go to any desk.

steps.p: If most tokens pick the same few experts, those GPUs are overloaded while others idle. Training adds a penalty that encourages even use.
A single very long sequence can be split across GPUs. "Ring attention" passes chunks around a ring so each part can attend to all the others.
Good systems start sending data while still computing, so GPUs don't sit idle waiting for messages.

cards.q: Expert parallelism relies heavily on which communication pattern?
cards.why: All-to-all. Tokens on every GPU may need experts on every other GPU, so data is shuffled in every direction.

cards.q: Why do mixture-of-experts models add a load-balancing penalty during training?
options: To stop most tokens going to a few experts while others sit idle
cards.why: Even workloads. An overloaded expert slows everyone, and unused experts waste memory.

cards.statement: Ring attention lets attention over a very long sequence be split across many GPUs.
cards.why: True. Each GPU holds part of the sequence and passes its chunk around the ring, so every part eventually meets every other.

cards.title: DeepSeek wrote custom low-level GPU code to work around export-restricted chips.
cards.detail: Its H800 GPUs had slower chip-to-chip links. The V3 report describes custom communication code and a schedule that overlapped computing with data transfers.

cards.q: Why do training systems overlap communication with computation?
options: So GPUs keep computing while data moves, instead of waiting
cards.hint: Look at the comparison in step 5.
cards.why: No idle chips. Every second a GPU waits is wasted money. Overlapping hides the transfer time behind useful work.

steps.p: With tens of thousands of GPUs, cables and power supplies, a failure every few hours is normal — even if each part is very reliable.

visual.caption: Rough failures per day, scaled from Meta's Llama 3 run.

steps.p: The run saves checkpoints regularly. After a crash it restarts from the last one, losing only the work since then.
steps.analogy: Saving your game every few minutes because the power keeps cutting out.

steps.p: Writing hundreds of gigabytes takes time, so checkpoints are saved in the background while training continues.
Worst of all: faulty hardware that quietly returns wrong numbers without any error message. Teams run checks to spot suspicious results.
The largest runs now span multiple data centers, linked by fast long-distance networks.

options: Faulty hardware returns wrong results without raising any error
cards.why: No alarm. A crash is obvious. Wrong numbers that look normal can quietly damage the model for days.

cards.statement: On a cluster of tens of thousands of GPUs, an interruption every few hours is normal.
cards.why: True. Meta reported 419 unexpected interruptions in 54 days training Llama 3 — about one every three hours.

cards.q: Why do large runs save checkpoints in the background?
options: Writing hundreds of gigabytes would otherwise pause training
Because disks are slow to start
cards.why: No pausing. Stopping thousands of GPUs while a huge save finishes wastes a lot of expensive time.

cards.title: Google trained Gemini Ultra across multiple data centers at once.
cards.detail: Its 2023 report describes TPU pods in several facilities working on one run, linked by Google's network — an early example of multi-site training.

cards.title: Estimate training time
cards.body: Training compute ≈ 6 × parameters × tokens. Divide by (GPUs × each GPU's useful speed) to get seconds.
cards.challenge: Try it: a 7B model on 1 trillion tokens is about 4 × 10²² FLOPs. With 1,000 GPUs each doing a useful 4 × 10¹⁴ per second, how many hours?
